bibliographic.title: Characterizing emission factors and oxidative potential of motorcycle emissions in a real-world tunnel environment
bibliographic.funding: Taiwan Ministry of Science and Technology (now National Science and Technology Council), grant MOST 111-2111-M-002-008; Research Centre for Environmental Changes (RCEC), Academia Sinica, grant AS-GC-110-01. Competing interests: Hsiao reports the MOST and RCEC financial support.
bibliographic.openAccess: unknown (no open-access licence statement printed; footer reads 'Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved'). Data 'will be made available on request'.
bibliographic.citation: Ting, Y.-C., Chang, P.-K., Hung, P.-C., Chou, C.C.-K., Chi, K.-H., Hsiao, T.-C. (2023). Characterizing emission factors and oxidative potential of motorcycle emissions in a real-world tunnel environment. Environmental Research 234, 116601. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envres.2023.116601

studyDesign: Measurements were made 14 to 23 March 2020 in the Ziqiang Tunnel, Taipei, Taiwan: 819 m long, two bores through Jiannan Mountain, gradient uniformly below 5%, measured only in the north-to-south lane (p.3). Entrance in a suburban area of schools and housing; exit in an urban zone next to main roads. Two platforms 100 m inside entrance and exit. PM2.5 collected on 47 mm Teflon filters (ARA N-FRM samplers with sharp-cut cyclones, 16.7 L/min) over 24 h, 20 samples (10 days x entrance and exit). CO and CO2 by custom-made low-cost electrochemical and NDIR sensors. eBC from an AE33 aethalometer and a calibrated microAeth MA350 (880 nm, MAC 7.77 m2/g); AAE also computed. Vehicles counted by hand from video and classed as motorcycles (MC), light-duty vehicles (LDV, mainly cars) and heavy-duty vehicles (HDV). Emission factors per kg fuel (carbon balance, FCEF1) and per vehicle-km (VKEF2, from exit-minus-entrance concentration, flux and tunnel length, entrance and exit airflow assumed equal). Vehicle-type EFs from multiple linear regression of fleet EFs on vehicle fractions weighted by assumed fuel consumption (MC and LDV assumed gasoline, HDV diesel; MC and LDV fuel economy from 2018 ITRI new-vehicle specifications; HDV value borrowed from a Hong Kong study and scaled by an LDT fraction; Table S2, supplement not available to the checker). Oxidative potential by DTT assay on filter extracts, per air volume (OPv, nmol/min/m3) and per particle mass (OPm, pmol/min/ug). No VOC, hydrocarbon, benzene, NOx, particle-number, PAH, metal, OC/EC or source-apportionment measurements. No separation of two-stroke, four-stroke or electric motorcycles. Hourly diurnal profiles of CO, CO2, PM2.5 and eBC at the exit appear in Fig. 3-4; the hourly PM2.5 instrument is not described in the main text. Only the main text was available; the supplement (Table S2, Fig. S1) was not.

findings.claim: Real-world tunnel experiment in a mixed-traffic tunnel in Taipei, measured over 10 days in March 2020 at entrance and exit platforms (north-to-south lane only).
findings.value: 819 m tunnel; gradient <5%; platforms 100 m from entrance and exit; 14-23 March 2020; 20 PM2.5 filter samples (24 h each)
findings.quote: Over the tunnel's total length of 819 m, the gradient remains uniformly below 5%
findings.caveats: Only the north-to-south lane was measured. Short campaign, one tunnel. The paper does not describe tunnel ventilation or traffic speed. Not street level.
findings.useOnSite: A real-world tunnel in Taipei where roughly half the vehicles are motorcycles gives measured per-vehicle emission factors for Taiwanese traffic, but it is not a street-corner measurement.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected from 2 to 3 (Section 2 begins on p.3; p.2 holds Fig. 1 and the Introduction). Quote located at p.3.

findings.claim: On weekdays about half of vehicles in the tunnel were motorcycles; on weekends cars outnumbered them.
findings.value: Weekdays ~40,500 vehicles/day: 44.4% LDV, 51.8% MC, 3.8% HDV. Weekends >27,000/day: 54.0% LDV, 43.1% MC, 2.9% HDV
findings.quote: approximately 40,500 per day, consisting of 44.4% LDVs, 51.8% MCs, and 3.8% HDVs
findings.caveats: Manual video classification. Fuel type, engine stroke (two/four) and electric share are not reported; MCs are assumed gasoline (p.3). Table 2 (p.6) labels the fleet '45% Motorcycle' and '2~6% HDV', not explained by the text figures.
findings.useOnSite: Motorcycles were about half of the tunnel's traffic (about 52% on weekdays); the paper does not say how many were electric.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers and page confirmed against text and Fig. 3 (weekday peak about 6,500 veh/h at 08:00 on the plot).

findings.claim: Motorcycles were the largest share of traffic at both weekday rush hours (about 61%); morning peak above 6,000 vehicles per hour.
findings.value: MC ~61.3% of traffic at both weekday rush hours; morning peak >6000 veh/h; morning-rush MC count 3.8x higher on weekdays than weekends (LDV 2.9x, HDV 1.7x)
findings.quote: MCs accounted for the highest proportion of traffic volume among vehicle types at both rush hours, at approximately 61.3%
findings.caveats: Traffic counts, not exposure. Morning rush (07:00-09:00) is about twice evening rush (16:00-18:00). Elsewhere the text says MCs were 'more than 50%' of both rush hours.
findings.useOnSite: At the weekday rush hours about six in ten vehicles in this Taipei tunnel were motorcycles.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed. Authors attribute it to commuters riding motorcycles (their statement, no data).

findings.claim: PM2.5 at the tunnel exit was higher than at the entrance by about 8 ug/m3 (24-h filter averages).
findings.value: Entrance 15.75 +/- 5.90 ug/m3; exit 23.81 +/- 5.21 ug/m3; difference 8.06 +/- 1.96 ug/m3 (weekday difference 8.95 +/- 0.29; weekend 6.95 +/- 2.68)
findings.locator: Section 3.1.2 (means on p.4, weekday/weekend differences on p.5)
findings.quote: 15.75 +/- 5.90 and 23.81 +/- 5.21 (ug/m3), respectively (Fig. S1)
findings.significance: No significance test printed for entrance versus exit. The '+/-' is not defined (SD or SE).
findings.caveats: 24-h filter averages inside a tunnel, not street-level concentrations. The increment correlated most with HDV flow (r = 0.78, p<0.01), not with motorcycles. Fig. 3 plots hourly exit PM2.5 of roughly 33-48 ug/m3 (weekday) read off the axis, well above the 23.81 filter mean; the main text does not say what instrument produced the hourly series.
findings.useOnSite: Air at the tunnel exit carried about 8 ug/m3 more PM2.5 than the entrance, from the traffic inside, mostly attributed to heavy vehicles.
findings.checkerNote: Page range and numbers confirmed. Caveats added: undefined +/-, and the unexplained gap between Fig. 3 hourly PM2.5 and the filter means (my reading of the plot, approximate).

findings.claim: PM2.5 and eBC in the tunnel tracked heavy-duty vehicle flow most strongly, not motorcycles.
findings.value: PM2.5 vs HDV flow r = 0.85 (p<0.05); PM2.5 vs other vehicle types and total flow r = 0.49-0.56 (p<0.01); PM2.5 increment vs HDV r = 0.78 (p<0.01); eBC vs HDV r = 0.86 (p<0.01)
findings.quote: the correlation between PM2.5 and HDV flow reached 0.85 (p-value <0.05)
findings.significance: p<0.05 for the 0.85 versus p<0.01 for the weaker values, as printed (odd given the larger r).
findings.caveats: Correlations of vehicle flow with concentrations at the exit; the paper does not say the time resolution or n (the reader's 'hourly series' is an inference from Fig. 3, which shows average diurnal profiles). Correlation, not causation. Abstract states HDVs dominated PM2.5 and eBC.
findings.useOnSite: In this tunnel, particle pollution tracked the number of heavy diesel vehicles, not motorcycles.
findings.checkerNote: Corrected: 'hourly series' removed as unsupported; pages are 4 and 6 (not 4-5; the eBC correlation is on p.6).

findings.claim: Tunnel CO correlated best with motorcycle flow and CO2 best with car flow.
findings.value: MC vs CO r = 0.96 (p<0.01), MC vs CO2 r = 0.86; LDV vs CO2 r = 0.95, LDV vs CO r = 0.83 (all p<0.01)
findings.quote: MCs have a higher correlation with CO (r = 0.96, p-value <0.01) than CO2 (r = 0.86, p-value <0.01)
findings.caveats: Correlation with flow, not an emission factor; MC and LDV flows themselves co-vary. The 'higher combustion efficiency of LDVs' explanation is the authors' reasoning, not measured.
findings.useOnSite: Carbon monoxide in the tunnel rose and fell with motorcycle numbers (r = 0.96).
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed. CO and CO2 concentrations appear only in Fig. 3 (see added finding).

findings.claim: eBC at the tunnel exit exceeded the entrance by 2 to 6 ug/m3, peaking at rush hours.
findings.value: Exit minus entrance eBC 2-6 ug/m3; exit peaks 08:00-09:00 and 17:00-18:00
findings.quote: differences in eBC concentrations between the exit and entrance ranging from 2 to 6 (ug/m3)
findings.caveats: Mean eBC not printed in text; Fig. 4a (read off the plot, approximate): weekday exit about 6-10 ug/m3, entrance about 2.5-7; weekend exit about 4-7, entrance about 2-3.5. The right-hand panel of Fig. 4 is also titled 'Weekday' on the plot though it appears to be weekend data. Strong correlation is with HDVs.
findings.useOnSite: The black carbon at the exit was 2 to 6 ug/m3 higher than at the entrance, mainly linked to heavy vehicles.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected from 5 to 6 (text of 3.1.4 is on p.6; Fig. 4 is on p.5).

findings.claim: The absorption Angstrom exponent (AAE) was 1.1 to 1.3, which the authors say resembles fossil-fuel combustion; exit air was dominated by fresh in-tunnel emissions.
findings.value: AAE 1.1-1.3 (text); fossil-fuel eBC AAE about 1.0, BrC 1.4 or higher (paper's own benchmarks)
findings.quote: The AAE range during the sampling period in this study was between 1.1 and 1.3
findings.caveats: Fig. 4b shows the weekend evening entrance AAE rising to about 1.43 (read off the plot), above the text range and above the paper's 1.4 BrC benchmark. AAE at the entrance dropped in morning rush and rose in evening, attributed by authors to outside traffic and aged air.
findings.useOnSite: Optical data point to fossil-fuel combustion; they do not identify motorcycles.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected 5 to 6 (Methods benchmark on p.3). Added the figure/text mismatch.

findings.claim: Fleet-average fuel-based emission factors for the whole tunnel fleet (about 45% motorcycles per Table 1).
findings.value: eBC 0.046 +/- 0.017 g/kg-fuel; PM2.5 0.131 +/- 0.013 g/kg-fuel (Table 1; text prints 0.130); CO 0.108 +/- 0.026 kg/kg-fuel; CO2 2.940 +/- 0.073 kg/kg-fuel
findings.caveats: Mixed fleet, not motorcycle-only. CO and CO2 are kg per kg fuel (superscript b). Carbon-balance method depends on assumed fuel carbon fraction (Table S2, supplement). The comparison rows in Table 1 for CO are Houston LDV 0.058-0.082 and Aberdeen 0.029 +/- 0.010 kg/kg-fuel.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed including the 0.130/0.131 discrepancy between text and Table 1.

findings.claim: Fleet-average distance-based emission factors; the authors say CO was higher than in previous tunnel studies, which they attribute to motorcycles.
findings.caveats: Per average vehicle of a fleet that was roughly half motorcycles. Text says VKEF CO is 'higher' than Mancilla and Mendoza, McGaughey, Zhang 2015 and Zhao 2018 'which might be due to the high traffic flow of MCs and the poor combustion efficiency of locomotive engines' (hypothesis, no motorcycle-free comparison). Table 2 gives CO only for Zhujiang (Zhang 2015): 3.10 g/veh/km, which is not lower than 3.08 here. The Methods compute VKEF directly (Eq. 4) but p.6 says the VKEF were 'converted' from FCEF1; the paper does not reconcile these.
findings.useOnSite: The fleet's CO per vehicle-km was about 3.1 g, similar to one earlier Chinese tunnel; the paper's explanation that motorcycles raise it is a hypothesis.
findings.checkerNote: Claim softened: 'higher than previous tunnel studies' is the authors' statement but Table 2 does not show it for the one tunnel with a listed CO value. Added the Eq. 4 versus 'converted' inconsistency.

findings.claim: Per kg of fuel burned, motorcycles emitted about ten times the CO of cars in this tunnel; the heavy-duty value is not distinguishable from zero.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Ziqiang, CO row; columns LDV, MC, HDV)
findings.significance: Authors: EF differences among vehicle types significant at p<0.05 for eBC, CO and CO2 (p.7); test not specified.
findings.caveats: Regression-derived. MC/LDV ratio about 9.5 is the checker's arithmetic, not printed. LDV uncertainty (+/-0.019) is about 86% of its value, so the ratio is imprecise. HDV (+/-0.127 on 0.014) is not distinguishable from zero. Gasoline assumed for all MCs; stroke type unknown.
findings.useOnSite: In this tunnel's regression, motorcycles emitted several times more CO per litre of fuel than cars, a point estimate with wide error on the car value.
findings.checkerNote: Original 'far more than heavy-duty' softened because the HDV estimate has uncertainty about nine times its value; added LDV uncertainty note.

findings.claim: Per kilometre driven, a motorcycle emitted about twice the CO of a car in the tunnel.
findings.caveats: Ratio about 2.1 is the checker's arithmetic. Table 4 comparisons for MC CO: Chen 2003 Taiwan on-road 7.65 +/- 2.91 g/km; Tung 2011 Vietnam 12.09 (LDV 1.88); Lin 2019 dynamometer 3.68-14.2. Gap per km is smaller than per kg fuel because fuel economy for MCs was assumed from 2018 new-vehicle specifications. HDV +/-4.31 exceeds its value.
findings.useOnSite: A motorcycle emitted roughly twice a car's CO per kilometre in this tunnel (4.3 versus 2.1 g/km); older on-road and dynamometer studies cited in the same table found more.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed against the page image of Table 4.

findings.claim: Motorcycles emitted the least CO2 per km and per kg fuel among the three vehicle classes.
findings.caveats: HDV uncertainty equals the value (VKEF). Authors explain by smaller size and more efficient engines of MCs (p.7).
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The regression found motorcycle PM2.5 and eBC emission factors to be the lowest of the three classes, with PM2.5 not distinguishable from zero.
findings.value: VKEF MC: eBC 0.16 +/- 0.37 mg/veh/km; PM2.5 0.46 +/- 31.20 mg/veh/km. FCEF MC: eBC 0.013 +/- 0.010 g/kg-fuel; PM2.5 0.013 +/- 0.143 g/kg-fuel
findings.significance: Authors' p<0.05 vehicle-type test is stated for eBC, CO and CO2 only.
findings.caveats: The MC PM2.5 uncertainty is about 70 times the estimate and the eBC uncertainty exceeds its value. The paper cannot support a claim that gasoline motorcycles emit a lot of PM2.5 or black carbon; its point estimate shows the opposite.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use this paper for motorcycle particle emissions; it does not show them to be high.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed against page image.

findings.claim: Heavy-duty vehicles emitted far more particles than cars or motorcycles (authors' printed ratios).
findings.value: FCEF ratios: eBC HDV/LDV 22.42, HDV/MC 50.92; PM2.5 HDV/LDV 18.88, HDV/MC 159.54. VKEF ratios: eBC HDV/LDV 6.80, HDV/MC 83.65; PM2.5 HDV/LDV 5.53, HDV/MC 69.45
findings.quote: were 22.42, 50.92, 18.88 and 159.54, respectively
findings.significance: The PM2.5 ratios rest on estimates with huge uncertainty (HDV VKEF PM2.5 32.09 +/- 292.28; MC 0.46 +/- 31.20), so they are not statistically meaningful; the eBC ratios are better constrained (HDV eBC 13.05 +/- 3.00).
findings.caveats: Ratios recomputed from tables (e.g. 13.05/0.16 = 81.6 vs printed 83.65) differ slightly, probably rounding. HDV vehicle count excludes any LDT/HDV split (LDTs possibly ~70% of the HDV count, p.3), so 'HDV' here may largely be light trucks.
findings.checkerNote: Added the uncertainty caveat for PM2.5 ratios and the LDT/HDV classification caveat.

findings.claim: The authors describe motorcycle CO as a poisonous gas and flag high motorcycle flow as a concern for health, air quality and climate.
findings.value: n/a (qualitative)
findings.quote: the high emission of CO and CO2 from MCs need to be paid attention to as the high flow of MCs will impact on the human health, air quality, and climate to a certain extent
findings.caveats: No health outcome or exposure was measured. The 'poisonous gas' wording is generic (p.7: 'which is a poisonous gas and plays an important role in the formation of tropospheric ozone').
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The authors cite another study saying motorcycles collectively emit 16 times more hydrocarbons and three times more CO than passenger cars.
findings.value: 16x hydrocarbons, 3x CO (cited)
findings.quote: MCs collectively emit 16 times more hydrocarbons, three times more carbon monoxide, and a 'disproportionately high' amount of other air pollutants compared to passenger cars
findings.caveats: Not measured in this paper; hydrocarbons were not measured here. The following sentence ('Both two- and four-stroke motorcycle engines emit significantly more of these pollutants than automobile engines') carries no separate citation in the printed text.
findings.checkerNote: Reader said the second sentence was 'also cited'; the text shows no separate citation, so treat it as continuing the Vasic and Weilenmann attribution only if checked against that source.

findings.claim: Fleet PM2.5 emission factors were comparable with or lower than earlier tunnel studies.
findings.value: This study VKEF2 PM2.5 4.07 mg/veh/km vs Loma Larga 9.30, Zhujiang (He 2008) 52.00, Hatfield 14.30, Kaisermuhlen 46.80; Zhujiang (Zhang 2015) 4.40-310
findings.quote: VKEF2PM2.5 of the Loma Larga tunnel ... and Zhujiang tunnel ... were twice or even higher than that of this study
findings.caveats: Authors summarise as 'comparable'. Per-vehicle PM2.5 here was low relative to most earlier tunnels, which cuts against any argument that a motorcycle-rich fleet is a PM2.5 hotspot.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed against Table 2.

findings.claim: The authors note the emission factors might include non-exhaust sources but did not examine them.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: the EFs mentioned might also be influenced by non-exhaust traffic emissions, such as road dust resuspension, tire abrasion, and brake wear. However, this study does not delve into these specifics.
findings.caveats: No chemical speciation (OC/EC, metals) was done, so brake and tyre wear versus exhaust cannot be separated.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The summed vehicle-type emission factors matched the bulk fleet emission factor within 10%.
findings.value: error <10%
findings.quote: the errors between the sum of the emission factors for each vehicle type derived by multiple linear regression and the bulk emission factor was less than 10%
findings.caveats: A self-consistency check, not independent validation.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed (sentence begins p.7, ends p.8).

findings.claim: Volume-based oxidative potential (DTT) of tunnel PM2.5 fell within the range reported at other urban and traffic sites.
findings.value: OPDTTv 0.15-0.46 nmol/min/m3; comparison sites 0.04-3.70 (Atlanta Freeway) to 2.10-9.30 (Tehran)
findings.quote: the OPDTTv obtained in the present study ranged between 0.15 and 0.46 nmol/min/m3
findings.caveats: Ten daily samples at each end; no mean or confidence interval printed (only per-day points in Fig. 5). Entrance and exit are not labelled separately in Table 5. Fig. 5 values consistent with the range (exit 14 March about 0.455; lowest about 0.15).
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed against Fig. 5 and Table 5.

findings.claim: Mass-based oxidative potential was reported as 27 to 101 pmol/min/ug, which the authors call similar to the Caldecott Tunnel and a US highway.
findings.value: OPDTTm 27.21-100.68 pmol/min/ug; Caldecott 68.0-75.0; Atlanta Freeway 73.0 +/- 72.0; Los Angeles freeways 30.1 +/- 3.15; Tehran 20.5-41.5; Xi'an 6.89-15.7
findings.quote: ranged between 27.21 and 100.68 pmol/min/ug in this study
findings.caveats: Fig. 5 shows an entrance OPm point on 21 March of roughly 230 pmol/min/ug (read off the left axis), outside the printed range, which the text does not mention. The study's upper bound is the highest of all rows in Table 5. No OP emission factors are printed in the main text although the Introduction says it will calculate 'OPDTT-based EFs'.
findings.checkerNote: Added the Fig. 5 point outside the printed range and the fact this study's upper OPm bound tops Table 5; the 'similar to Caldecott/US highway' wording is the authors'.

findings.claim: Per unit mass, particles at the tunnel exit (fresh emissions) generally had lower oxidative potential than entrance particles (aged air), while per unit air volume the exit was generally higher.
findings.value: OPDTTv exit generally > entrance; OPDTTm exit < entrance (Fig. 5); no numeric means printed
findings.quote: the OPDTTm at the exit was lower than at the entrance, possibly due to the transition of PM2.5 chemical compositions
findings.caveats: Explanation (freshness, PAH oxidation) is the authors' hypothesis ('It was, therefore, hypothesized'); no chemical composition was measured. Fig. 5 shows overlap on some days (e.g. 20 March) and one entrance OPm outlier. No statistical test reported. This weakens any claim that fresh tailpipe PM is especially toxic per microgram.
findings.useOnSite: The paper found freshly emitted traffic particles were not more potent per microgram than aged air at the tunnel entrance; its volume-based OP was higher at the exit because there were more particles.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed. The 'more particles' explanation for higher OPv is arithmetic (OPv = OPm x mass) and consistent with the authors' text; the paper does not state it so.

findings.claim: Oxidative potential is a measure of the extent of oxidative stress that particles can induce through reactive oxygen species; the DTT assay measures how fast particles consume DTT.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: oxidation potential (OP) of PM, which measures the extent of oxidative stress induced by reactive oxygen species
findings.caveats: OP is a laboratory proxy, not a health outcome. Paper says DTT has been 'closely linked to adverse health effects' without citation in that sentence.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The authors state that inhaling traffic-related PM2.5 can lead to oxidative stress, inflammation and tissue and DNA damage.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: inhalation exposure to traffic-related PM2.5 can lead to oxidative stress, inflammation, and tissue and DNA damage to the human respiratory system
findings.caveats: General statement, not a result of this study; no citation attached to that sentence.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The authors conclude fresh PM2.5 contributes less to OP than aged particles, yet volume-based OP indicates health impact cannot be ignored.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: fresh traffic emissions were less toxic than aged aerosols, but higher OPDTTv indicated the impact on human health cannot be ignored
findings.caveats: Not a population health result. The paper has no epidemiology, and no data on children, older people, riders or pedestrians. The Conclusions add that aged aerosols 'cause more significant health hazards' (p.9), an inference from OP, not a measured outcome.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The authors conclude that, because motorcycle flow is the highest, total emissions from motorcycles are not negligible, especially in Southeast Asia.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: Accompanied with the highest traffic flow, the total emissions of air pollutants from MCs are not negligible, especially in the Southeast Asian countries with large numbers of MCs.
findings.caveats: The Conclusions identify MCs as the highest CO emitters, HDVs as the highest PM2.5 and eBC emitters, and call for 'reducing the proportion of HDVs'. 'Highest traffic flow' is true only at weekday rush hours (MC 51.8% weekday, 43.1% weekend).
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The Introduction cites that motorcycles are a large share of the vehicle fleet in several Asian countries including Taiwan.
findings.value: Printed: '74.6%, 69.6%, and 69.6% of the vehicle fleet in Indonesia, Taiwan, India, and Thailand, respectively' (three figures for four countries)
findings.quote: They comprise 74.6%, 69.6%, and 69.6% of the vehicle fleet in Indonesia, Taiwan, India, and Thailand, respectively (Chemonics International, 2000)
findings.caveats: Three percentages for four countries (printing error); source is a 2000 USAID/Egypt Cairo project report per the reference list. Do not use on the site without checking the source.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed.

findings.claim: The Introduction cites chassis-dynamometer work saying motorcycle tailpipe emissions differ from light-duty vehicles in CO/CO2 and hydrocarbons, and may link greater hydrocarbon emissions to more secondary organic aerosol.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: motorcycle tailpipe emissions exhibit distinctly different CO/CO2 and hydrocarbon (HC) concentrations based on chassis dynamometer studies
findings.caveats: Cited (Hassani et al., 2021; Platt et al., 2014), not measured here.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed (sentence on p.1; SOA clause runs onto p.2).

findings.claim: Fuel-based particle emission factors by vehicle class (Table 3): the motorcycle estimates are the lowest and PM2.5 is not distinguishable from zero.
findings.caveats: Regression-derived, '+/-' undefined. Reader did not capture these cells.
findings.useOnSite: Same message as the per-km table: this paper does not show gasoline motorcycles to be a large particle source.
findings.checkerNote: Added because the reader's chart only had the per-km particle values.

findings.claim: Exit concentrations of CO and CO2 are plotted in Fig. 3 (not printed in text); CO peaks near 20 ppm and CO2 near 760 ppm at the weekday morning rush hour.
findings.value: Weekday exit, read off Fig. 3 (approximate): CO about 20 ppm at 08:00, about 0-5 ppm overnight; CO2 about 430 ppm overnight to about 760 ppm at 08:00; weekend CO2 about 450-620 ppm
findings.quote: (figure only; no printed number)
findings.caveats: Values are the checker's reading of a plot, accurate to perhaps +/- 10%; do not quote as the paper's numbers. Sensors are custom low-cost devices with no calibration detail in the main text. Exit values only; no entrance CO or CO2 shown. The hourly PM2.5 in the same figure (about 33-48 ug/m3 on weekdays) is higher than the 24-h filter exit mean (23.81 ug/m3); instrument not described.
findings.useOnSite: Tunnel CO rose with the morning motorcycle-heavy rush hour, but exact concentrations are not given in the text.
findings.checkerNote: Added to answer question 2 on CO and CO2 concentrations; flagged as plot readings.

findings.claim: Table 4 also lists earlier motorcycle PM2.5 values from other studies that are very low, in line with this study's low motorcycle PM point estimate.
findings.value: Hatfield (UK) Lawrence 2016 MC PM2.5 0.001-0.0003 mg/veh/km (LDV 2.4-3.0, HDV 2.2-2.8); Lin 2019 dynamometer MC PM2.5 0.0167-0.479 mg/veh/km
findings.caveats: Cited values, not measured here; Lin 2019 is a dynamometer study. The paper does not discuss why MC PM2.5 is low.
findings.checkerNote: Complicates the site's particle argument: the literature the paper tabulates agrees that per-km motorcycle PM2.5 mass is small.

findings.claim: The paper does not define the '+/-' on emission factors or give the test behind its vehicle-type significance claim.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: The derived emission factors of eBC, CO and CO2 for three types of vehicles showed a significant difference in this study (p value < 0.05).
findings.caveats: No statement whether +/- is SD, SE or CI; no named test; PM2.5 is excluded from the significance statement. EFs 'were calculated with and without accounting for fuel consumption' (p.3) but only one set is shown in the main text.
findings.checkerNote: A sceptical reader cannot tell how precise the vehicle-type EFs are.

findings.claim: The Conclusions say eBC correlated with all vehicle types, especially HDVs, and that a high proportion of HDVs and MCs went with lower AAE values.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: eBC demonstrated a high correlation with all types of vehicles, especially with HDVs, indicating the necessity of reducing the proportion of HDVs
findings.caveats: The authors' policy recommendation arising from the data is to reduce HDV share; there is no motorcycle-reduction or electrification recommendation anywhere in the paper. The AAE claim is not backed by numbers in the text.
findings.checkerNote: The paper's own mitigation message is about HDVs, which matters for how the site cites it.

limitations: No dedicated limitations section. Stated or implied by the authors: (a) EFs 'might also be influenced by non-exhaust traffic emissions, such as road dust resuspension, tire abrasion, and brake wear. However, this study does not delve into these specifics' (p.6); (b) vehicle flow data 'did not distinguish between light-duty trucks (LDTs) and HDVs', with a post-survey suggesting LDTs might be ~70% of the HDV count (p.3); (c) no published HDV fuel economy for Taiwan was found; a Hong Kong diesel value scaled by the LDT fraction was used (p.3); (d) MC and LDV fuel economy came from 2018 'new vehicle' specifications and fuel use per type was assumed constant over time (p.3); (e) EFs vary with 'driving modes, fuel type, load, vehicle age, emission control technologies installed' and meteorology (p.6).
Checker: 10 days, one tunnel, one lane, PM2.5 only as 24-h filters (20 samples), so OP has about 10 points per site and no statistics compare entrance and exit.
Checker: CO and CO2 from custom low-cost sensors; the main text gives no calibration or accuracy detail.
Checker: entrance and exit airflow assumed equal for VKEF; tunnel ventilation and traffic speed are not described.
Checker: MC PM2.5 and eBC regression estimates have uncertainties as large as or far larger than the estimates (0.46 +/- 31.20 mg/veh/km); the meaning of +/- is not defined.
Checker: motorcycles assumed gasoline; no stroke, emission-standard stage, age or electric breakdown; vehicle categories coarse.
Checker: no hydrocarbon, VOC, benzene, NOx, particle-number, PAH, metal or OC/EC data, so particle composition and the cause of OP differences are speculation.
Checker: confined tunnel traffic; idling at red lights and congestion at crosswalks are not studied.
Checker: Fig. 3 hourly exit PM2.5 (about 33-48 ug/m3 on weekdays by plot reading) is not reconciled with the 24-h filter exit mean of 23.81 ug/m3.
complications: Motorcycle PM2.5 and eBC emission factors were the lowest of three classes (0.46 mg/veh/km PM2.5 and 0.16 mg/veh/km eBC versus HDV 32.09 and 13.05 and LDV 5.81 and 1.92), with PM2.5 uncertainty (+/-31.20) swamping the estimate; Table 4's cited literature also lists very low motorcycle PM2.5 (Hatfield 0.001-0.0003 mg/km). The paper does not show gasoline motorcycles to be major particle emitters.

The authors conclude heavy-duty vehicles dominated PM2.5 and eBC and call for reducing HDV share; the PM2.5 increment correlated with HDV flow (r = 0.78) rather than motorcycles. No electrification or motorcycle-reduction recommendation is made.
Motorcycle CO per km (4.33 g/veh/km) is only about twice the car value (2.06) and below the earlier on-road motorcycle values in Table 4 (7.65, 12.09 g/km).

Attribution of high fleet CO to motorcycles is inference from correlation and regression; no motorcycle-free comparison. Table 2 gives the one earlier tunnel CO value (Zhujiang 3.10 g/veh/km) as not lower than this study's 3.08.

Fresh exit particles had lower mass-based OP than aged entrance particles; the authors read this as fresh emissions being less toxic per microgram. Higher OPv at the exit follows from more particle mass.

OPv 0.15-0.46 nmol/min/m3 sits within most other sites' ranges and below Tehran's 2.10-9.30, so tunnel air is not extraordinary by this metric; OPm upper bound (100.68, plus a roughly 230 point in Fig. 5 outside the printed range) is the highest in Table 5.
Concentrations inside an 819 m tunnel are not street-level or crosswalk concentrations; the PM2.5 increment of about 8 ug/m3 is a 24-h average.
The paper contains nothing on electric motorcycles, children, strollers, older people, riders or roadside workers, idling, or health outcomes. No benzene or hydrocarbon was measured.

Table 2 labels the fleet '45% Motorcycle' while the text gives 51.8% (weekdays) and 43.1% (weekends); the Introduction lists three percentages for four countries; the text says VKEF CO is higher than Zhang 2015 but Table 2 shows 3.10 versus 3.08; the 0.130 versus 0.131 PM2.5 FCEF; Fig. 4 text AAE range 1.1-1.3 versus about 1.43 in Fig. 4b; Fig. 4's right panel titled 'Weekday'.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: Abstract-level note that the CO emission factor was higher than earlier studies is confirmed as the authors' statement, with numbers: fleet VKEF2 CO 3.076 +/- 0.675 g/veh/km (Table 2, p.6) and FCEF1 0.108 +/- 0.026 kg/kg-fuel (Table 1). But the attribution to motorcycles is the authors' explanation ('likely owing to the increased fraction of MCs', abstract), not a tested result, and Table 2 shows only Zhujiang 3.10 for comparison, which is not lower.
Vehicle-specific CO values are now known: MC 4.33 +/- 0.42, LDV 2.06 +/- 0.47, HDV 1.23 +/- 4.31 g/veh/km (Table 4); 0.209, 0.022, 0.014 kg/kg-fuel (Table 3).
The abstract could be read as supporting motorcycles as a particle source; the full text shows MC lowest and HDV highest for PM2.5 and eBC.
The main OP finding is that fresh exit PM had lower OPm than aged entrance PM; no OP emission factors per vehicle type are printed and no composition data support a driver of OP.
The tunnel is mixed traffic (about 52% MC on weekdays, 43% on weekends), not motorcycle-only; no stroke or electric breakdown.

answersToQuestions: 1. Ziqiang Tunnel, Taipei; 819 m, two bores through Jiannan Mountain, gradient <5%, only north-to-south lane measured (p.3); entrance suburban (schools, housing), exit urban (main roads). Mixed traffic: weekdays ~40,500 vehicles/day, 44.4% LDV, 51.8% MC, 3.8% HDV; weekends >27,000/day, 54.0% LDV, 43.1% MC, 2.9% HDV (p.4); MC ~61.3% at weekday rush hours, peak >6000 veh/h. Table 2 labels fleet '45% Motorcycle', '2~6% HDV'. No two-stroke, four-stroke or electric split; MCs and LDVs assumed gasoline, HDVs diesel (p.3). 14-23 March 2020; platforms 100 m inside each end; 24-h PM2.5 filters (20), low-cost CO/CO2 sensors, AE33/MA350 for eBC, manual video counts.

2. Numbers in text: PM2.5 entrance 15.75 +/- 5.90, exit 23.81 +/- 5.21 ug/m3, difference 8.06 +/- 1.96 (weekday 8.95 +/- 0.29, weekend 6.95 +/- 2.68) (pp.4-5); eBC exit minus entrance 2-6 ug/m3 (p.6); AAE 1.1-1.3 (p.6). CO and CO2 concentrations only plotted in Fig. 3 (checker reading: exit CO up to about 20 ppm, CO2 up to about 760 ppm at weekday morning rush; approximate). Flow correlations: PM2.5-HDV 0.85, CO-MC 0.96, CO2-LDV 0.95. Not measured: particle number, NOx, VOCs, metals, PAHs.

3. Fleet FCEF1 (Table 1): eBC 0.046 +/- 0.017, PM2.5 0.131 +/- 0.013 g/kg-fuel (text 0.130), CO 0.108 +/- 0.026, CO2 2.940 +/- 0.073 kg/kg-fuel. Fleet VKEF2 (Table 2): eBC 1.530 +/- 0.604, PM2.5 4.073 +/- 0.563 mg/veh/km, CO 3.076 +/- 0.675, CO2 96.364 +/- 24.404 g/veh/km. By type (Table 4, g/veh/km for CO, CO2; mg/veh/km for PM): CO MC 4.33, LDV 2.06, HDV 1.23; CO2 MC 45.85, LDV 138.91, HDV 124.37; eBC MC 0.16, LDV 1.92, HDV 13.05; PM2.5 MC 0.46 +/- 31.20, LDV 5.81, HDV 32.09 +/- 292.28. Table 3 fuel-based: CO MC 0.209, LDV 0.022, HDV 0.014 kg/kg-fuel; eBC 0.013, 0.031, 0.684 g/kg; PM2.5 0.013, 0.111, 2.087 g/kg. Authors: fleet EFs 'comparable' to earlier studies, CO higher (attributed to MCs), CO2 lower, PM2.5 of Loma Larga and Zhujiang twice or more. Passenger-car comparison is the LDV column; MC CO higher, MC PM and eBC lower. No comparison with emission standards.

4. DTT assay: OPv 0.15-0.46 nmol/min/m3; OPm 27.21-100.68 pmol/min/ug (p.8, Table 5; Fig. 5 also shows an entrance OPm point near 230 outside that range), similar per the authors to Caldecott 68.0-75.0 and other urban/traffic sites. Exit had generally higher OPv and lower OPm than entrance (Fig. 5), hypothesised as fresh particles being less potent per mass than aged ones; no composition measured so the driver of OP is untested; no source-specific OP or OP emission factors are given. Plain sentence: oxidative potential is a laboratory measure of how readily particles trigger oxidative stress (reactive oxygen chemistry) and is used as a proxy for how harmful they might be, not a measured health outcome.

5. Not measured: no OC, EC, metals, PAHs or ions. Only optical eBC (880 nm) and AAE 1.1-1.3 (consistent with fossil-fuel combustion). Brake/tyre wear versus exhaust cannot be separated; authors note non-exhaust sources may influence EFs and did not examine them (p.6).

6. Authors: 'the high emission of CO and CO2 from MCs need to be paid attention to as the high flow of MCs will impact on the human health, air quality, and climate to a certain extent' (p.7); 'inhalation exposure to traffic-related PM2.5 can lead to oxidative stress, inflammation, and tissue and DNA damage to the human respiratory system' (p.8); 'the total emissions of air pollutants from MCs are not negligible, especially in the Southeast Asian countries with large numbers of MCs' (p.9); 'freshly emitted PM2.5 from vehicles contributed less to OP compared to aged particles' (p.9); and 'the necessity of reducing the proportion of HDVs' (p.9). No health outcome was studied.
7. Nothing on rider exposure, idling or congestion (only tunnel traffic flow), electric motorcycles (MCs assumed gasoline), pedestrians, children or older people.

8. Stated: non-exhaust sources not examined; LDT and HDV not distinguished (LDTs possibly ~70% of HDV count); HDV fuel economy borrowed from Hong Kong; MC/LDV fuel economy from 2018 new-vehicle specs held constant; EFs depend on driving mode, age, controls, meteorology. Checker-added: 10-day single-tunnel single-lane campaign; 20 PM2.5 filters; low-cost CO/CO2 sensors without calibration detail; equal airflow assumption; MC PM2.5 and eBC uncertainties larger than values; undefined +/-; no stroke or standard breakdown; no VOC, benzene, NOx, number, metals or PAH data; no OP statistics.
